metadata.title: Predictive Machine Learning Approach for Complex Problem Solving Process Data Mining

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 computer-based assessment (CBA) log-file data for the Climate Control problem-solving unit (CP025Q01) and combines it with scored cognitive item response data to create a binary success outcome. The manuscript describes preprocessing (extracting relevant task entries, cleaning corrupted entries, and downsampling to balance classes) but does not report whether PISA complex survey weights were applied. Because the analysis is based on standard ML classifiers (e.g., Random Forest, Gradient Boosted Trees, deep learning) and the paper does not mention weight-aware estimation, it is unclear whether sampling weights were used; analysts should default to using the official PISA student/sampling weights (and replicate weights if available) when reproducing results. If weights were omitted, this should be treated as a limitation because PISA sampling is clustered (students within schools) and unweighted ML can under/over-represent certain strata.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is the success/failure of solving the Climate Control task (binary classification derived from the scored cognitive item response), not a PV-based cognitive achievement score. Therefore, plausible values are not applicable to the modeled outcome. The paper also does not describe a missing-data strategy for the engineered time- and VOTAT-based features (e.g., how incomplete log sequences or missing timestamps were handled), which is a reporting gap given that log-based features can be missing when students disengage or do not complete all task phases.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2012 computer-based assessment Climate Control problem-solving task, restricting to the first question/unit item CP025Q01. Extracted relevant entries from (i) scored cognitive item response data and (ii) problem-solving log files containing slider positions, button clicks, and actions; assigned sequence order numbers and timestamps. After cleaning the data and eliminating corrupted entries, the success outcome was split into two classes and downsampling was applied to balance the classes; the final analytic dataset contained 15,194 entries.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 Grade 15-year-old (CBA) Climate Control CP025Q01 problem-solving process data
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model (deep learning, VOTAT-based features): Accuracy 94.9%, AUCROC 0.958, Recall 94.8%, F-measure 94.9% (Table 3). Baseline comparison (Table 1): Random Forest Accuracy 94.1%, AUC 0.950, F-measure 94.5%; Gradient Boosted Trees Accuracy 94.1%, AUC 0.950, F-measure 94.5%; Logistic Regression Accuracy 89.7%, AUC 0.933, F-measure 93.3%; Naive Bayes Accuracy 87.8%, AUC 0.920, F-measure 88.5%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Grade 15-year-old (CBA) Climate Control CP025Q01 problem-solving process data, the study leveraged VOTAT strategy usage features, control apply usage ratios, and total apply actions to predict Climate Control success, finding that deep learning achieved the highest F-measure (94.9%) and AUCROC (0.958) with VOTAT-based features. This indicates that students’ strategy enactment patterns in computer-based problem solving can be used to build highly accurate early-warning/assistance systems for complex problem-solving success, though the paper does not report survey-weighting or a missing-data strategy and uses downsampling for class balance.

data.outcome_summary: The study builds and compares six supervised ML classifiers (Naïve Bayes, logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, gradient boosted trees, and deep learning) to predict binary success on the PISA 2012 computer-based Climate Control problem-solving unit CP025Q01 using raw log-file process data. Two feature sets are evaluated: VOTAT-based action features (control apply usage ratios and total apply actions) and time-based paradata features (relative reading time, experiment/drawing time ratios, normalized total time, and apply speed). Across both feature sets, deep learning is the best-performing model: with VOTAT-based features it reaches F-measure 94.9% and AUCROC 0.958 (optimized network), while with time-based features it reaches F-measure 77.9% and AUCROC 0.857. The paper reports class balancing via downsampling and uses genetic-algorithm optimization of neural network structure, but it does not report a missing-data strategy or whether PISA complex survey weights were applied, limiting interpretability for population-level inference.
